slot.brief: Find the condition on k so that both roots of x² + px + k = 0 lie in a given interval (0,1); combine f(0)>0, f(1)>0, discriminant, vertex location.

stem: For what values of $k$ do both roots of $x^2-\dfrac{3}{2}x+k=0$ lie in $(0,1)$?

verdicts.working: Real roots require k≤9/16. Their product is positive for k>0, so both are positive. Also (1−r₁)(1−r₂)=k−1/2; since their sum is 3/2, both are below 1 exactly when k>1/2. Thus 1/2<k≤9/16.

working:
$f(0)=k>0,\quad f(1)=k-\dfrac12>0$. The vertex is at $x=\dfrac34\in(0,1)$; real roots require $\Delta=\dfrac94-4k\ge0$. Hence $\dfrac12<k\le\dfrac{9}{16}$.

Independent check: Real roots require k≤9/16. Their product is positive for k>0, so both are positive. Also (1−r₁)(1−r₂)=k−1/2; since their sum is 3/2, both are below 1 exactly when k>1/2. Thus 1/2<k≤9/16.
solution:
For roots $r_1,r_2$, their product is $k$ and $(1-r_1)(1-r_2)=k-\frac12$. Both roots are positive and less than $1$ when $k>\frac12$; real roots also require $\Delta=\frac94-4k\ge0$.
Thus $\frac12<k\le\frac9{16}$.
